take: Brent’s push to $107 as the UN disappoints and Iran threatens to widen the war to the Indian Ocean is the dominant story, with the Strait of Hormuz now a live physical risk after the Cape Dao was struck and a seafarer killed, so crude upside skew stays bid and the diesel complex is the cleanest expression given the record $6.52/gal national average and elevated crack spreads. Freight is the second theme and it is transmitting straight into delivered crude costs, with freight now roughly a fifth of a cargo’s cost and Japan’s imports the world’s most expensive, whilst Saudi’s Red Sea workaround carries war-risk premiums nearly as expensive as transiting Hormuz itself. On flows, the EIA’s 13.8mn b/d 2026 US production record and 17.4 Bcf/d H1 LNG export print keep the Atlantic Basin long crude and gas, so the squeeze is a freight-and-geopolitics trade rather than a supply-shortage one, and the mooted US diesel export ban would only reprice barrels rather than lower them. Cross-market, watch the gasoil–bunker spread and VLCC earnings against the Onex buying spree, as higher tanker rates feed directly into Asian crude CIF and bunker costs, with the FRED August recession probability at just 0.08% doing nothing to cap the risk premium. Next 24 hours: Hormuz transit and war-risk insurance quotes, any hardening of US diesel export restrictions, and whether Brent holds $107 into the weekly EIA inventory print.

items.title: Public companies produce most U.S. crude oil and natural gas
items.summary: Publicly traded companies represent a tiny share of the total number of companies producing crude oil and natural gas in the United States, but they make up a large share of U.S. production. In 2025, publicly traded companies accounted for just 2% of about 12,000 oil and natural gas producers but produced 68% of the crude oil and natural gas in the Lower 48 states.

items.title: What goes into diesel prices?
items.summary: The price of distillate fuel oil, often sold as diesel, is driven by the price of crude oil, retail margins, distribution costs, taxes, and crack spreads, the indicator we use for refining margins. Tight global supplies of distillate fuel oil and elevated crude oil prices have driven prices higher in recent months.
